description: We are a five-person team from Ukraine working on the Dancing with the SARs challenge. We use NISAR L-band radar to measure how forests recover after wildfires, starting with Canada. Optical satellites see green regrowth and overestimate recovery. Radar sees the actual forest structure, and we check our results against GEDI lidar. Our skills cover data science, ML, geospatial pipelines, backend and web development.
summary:
After a wildfire, satellite images usually show the burn turning green again within a few years. Optical indices such as NDVI see that green, but they cannot tell young shrubs from a forest that has grown back. This project uses the L-band radar of the NASA-ISRO NISAR mission, which is sensitive to trunks and branches, to show how far a burned forest has actually come back and when it is likely to be a forest again.

What the project does:
1. Shows fires that are already computed on a globe. For each fire it shows the forest height stage of every cell (under 5 m, 5-10 m, over 10 m), how recovered the fire is today compared with the unburned forest around it, and a forecast of when it reaches 80% of that height.
2. Compares three views of the same fire: what optics suggests, what our NISAR model says, and what GEDI lidar measured.
3. Lets a user find a fire in the catalog or draw an area, and runs the same pipeline for it.
*For now the model is calibrated and checked for Canada only. The map shows where it can be trusted elsewhere.
details:
How it works. For a fire perimeter from Canada’s NBAC catalog, the pipeline lays a 30 m grid over the burn and a 6 km ring of surrounding forest. It reads NISAR GCOV backscatter (HH, HV), Sentinel-1 backscatter (VH, VV) and Sentinel-2 NDVI from the same summer onto that grid. A regional state model turns these five values into a forest-height stage for each cell. GEDI space lidar measures the unburned forest 1.5-6 km around the fire, and that height defines “100% recovery”. A growth-curve model estimates when the fire reaches 80% of it. Everything is written as small JSON files that the frontend draws.

Benefits. The tool shows recovery as forest structure, not greenness, which is what matters for carbon, habitat and timber. In our four demo fires, optics suggested 83-94% recovery, while GEDI lidar measured far less in three of them. At fire level, our estimate differs from GEDI by about 12% (median, on fires not used in training), and we state this uncertainty openly. The forecast gives about 35-41 years to reach 80% in Canada. We label anything outside the 9-35-year range of fire ages we have data for as extrapolation.

Intended impact. We want forest managers, researchers and the public to have a more honest, checkable view of post-fire recovery than optical imagery alone. NISAR is new, and a tool that turns its data into a clear picture of the forest can show how L-band radar adds to optics. The pipeline runs for any fire polygon, so it can grow as NISAR coverage and validation data grow.

Tools.

  • Data: NASA NISAR L2 GCOV (Earthdata), Sentinel-1/2, GEDI L2A, NBAC, ESA WorldCover, Hansen Global Forest Change and MODIS burned area, via Google Earth Engine.
  • Code: Python (numpy, scipy, rasterio, shapely, pyproj, h5py, earthaccess, earthengine-api), a regional logistic-regression state model and a saturating-exponential growth model.
  • Backend and frontend: FastAPI, React, TypeScript, MapLibre and Three.js.

What is creative. We use lidar from space as ground truth to teach radar what a regrown forest looks like. We compare three views of one fire (optics, radar model, lidar), and we show where the model can and cannot be trusted. The stage colours avoid red-green so they work for colour-blind readers.

What we considered.

  • Seasons. We use summer scenes only, because snow and frozen trees break the radar signal.
  • Processing. We average radar in linear units before converting to dB, and every layer is computed on one shared grid.
  • Regions. We trained separate models per region, because one global model did not transfer. We tested each on a country the model had not seen, and Turkey’s result was only moderate (AUC 0.64).
  • Time gap. GEDI (2019-2023) and NISAR (2026) are years apart, so part of the difference is real growth.
  • Noise. Per-cell height is noisy (about ±3.7 m). So we show aggregates for each fire, and per cell only the stage and a relative score, not a calibrated probability.
  • Forecast scope. The growth forecast is confirmed only for Canada.
